summary: A new claim row reserves a plain-words pass on seven pages (net worth, debts, emergency fund, how am I doing, assumptions, mortgage and next best action), changing only wording, not figures.

An employer's match on a Roth 401(k) is now treated the way the law treats it: as money you pay the tax on later, unless your plan pays the match as Roth and you chose that. Your own contributions stay Roth, and the match goes into pay-the-tax-later money, stops when you stop work and counts toward required withdrawals.
points: Family example with a ,800 match: 83% of the money at retirement is pay-the-tax-later instead of 77%
Monthly income at retirement becomes ,656 instead of ,695
A new option keeps the old treatment for plans that pay the match as Roth, and the federal tax estimate then counts the match as income, 96 higher in the example
No sample household has such a row, so every other answer is unchanged
numbers: 96 more federal tax with a Roth match

summary: If you assume stocks, bonds or cash will earn more than our middle figures, the retirement answer other pages read now uses the middle figures whenever they give a worse result. A hopeful return can no longer turn a tight plan into an on-track one by itself.
points: A couple on 9% stocks is now told tight (3,333 a year for 8,680 needed) instead of on track (7,987)
A single saver with bonds at 7% is told the money runs out at 94, not tight
The money-lasting page keeps its hopeful answer but says underneath what the middle figures give
At the middle figures or below nothing changes
